evidence_quotes.quote: By water governance, I mean the bureaucratic management of the water infrastructure and the social control of water distribution within an irrigation system.
With the help of a local assistant, I conducted a survey among 100 households, which represented 18% of the 549 households that are members of Cabanaconde’s peasant community

A locally elected water committee now administers the new system, selling tickets to the villagers and thus authorizing those to claim water from the regidores, and whereas the village authorities previously appointed these regidores, the water committee now hires them.
according to my survey, the households now have an average of 1.75 ha of irrigated land compared with less than 1 ha before the community gained access to the Majes Canal.
In my 2011 survey, 97% of those interviewed affirmed that irrigation water is plentiful throughout the year

criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1 (Wrong service, E07). The paper exclusively examines agricultural irrigation water management and canal allocation for crop fields ('within an irrigation system', 'irrigate their fields'), not household or community drinking-water supply or sanitation service access. Although 'drinking water, domestic use' is mentioned once in passing as a general household background survey topic on p. 208, no analysis, governance mechanism, or outcome for domestic water or sanitation service is reported anywhere in the article.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines institutional and governance factors (adoption of a state water governance model, state grant of water rights from 4 valves in the Majes Canal, local water committees, and state-community relations), though solely in the context of agricultural irrigation rather than water/sanitation services. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although the paper describes local irrigation rules (ticket sales authorizing plot irrigation claims, water tariffs/fees, and formal water rights), it does not examine a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism governing household or community water supply or sanitation service access, and its primary analytical focus is macro-political opposition vs. cooperation between an Andean farming community and the state. Both plain and narrow readings yield overall exclusion because C1 and C4 fail on service scope (irrigation only).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies C3. Empirical ethnographic and survey case study based on 1 month of fieldwork in Cabanaconde in 2011, including a structured survey of 100 households (18% of 549 peasant community member households), formal interviews with community/business/religious leaders, life histories, participant observation, and canal infrastructure mapping.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4. Reported outcomes relate solely to agricultural irrigation and farmland (average irrigated land per household increasing from under 1 ha to 1.75 ha, expansion of community irrigated land by >1000 ha, 97% of respondents reporting plentiful irrigation water year-round, and reduced irrigation disputes), with no drinking-water or sanitation service access outcomes reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies C5. Population (peasant community households in Cabanaconde, Colca Valley, Peru; survey n = 100 of 549 households), exposure (grant of state canal water rights from the Majes Canal and shift from customary dual-moiety irrigation to a state water governance model), outcomes (agricultural irrigation availability and irrigated land area), and study design (ethnographic case study with household survey) are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies C6. Full text is published in English.

study_design: Mixed-methods ethnographic case study with cross-sectional household survey (n = 100 households), key-informant interviews, life histories, and participant observation
population_and_sample: Andean peasant community households and farmers in Cabanaconde, Arequipa region, Peru (population ~5,000; household survey n = 100 of 549 member households, plus key-informant interviews and participant observation)
exposure: Adoption of a state model of agricultural irrigation governance (local water committee selling irrigation tickets, hiring water distributors, paying user tariffs/fees) following state grant of water rights from 4 valves in the Majes Canal
outcome: Agricultural irrigation availability (97% reporting plentiful irrigation water throughout the year), irrigated landholdings per household (average 1.75 ha vs. <1 ha previously), and state-community cooperation in irrigation management
rationale: Excluded under E07 (Wrong service). Full-text review shows that Paerregaard (2013) is an empirical ethnographic and household-survey study exclusively examining agricultural canal irrigation governance, water allocation to crop fields, and irrigated farmland expansion in Cabanaconde, Peru. It does not examine household or community drinking-water supply or sanitation service access or report any domestic water or sanitation outcomes, so it is excluded under both the active narrow 2026-10-13 reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
